tur30-0: What scoliosis is, C and S curves, the Cobb angle, the risk of progression during the growth spurt; one-sided sitting and carrying habits, connective tissue flexibility; treatments from past to present, and a comparison of exercise, bracing and surgery.
tur30-2: One-sided habits and connective tissue flexibility
tur30-3: By one-sided habits we mean not only carrying a bag on one shoulder, but any habit that loads the trunk towards the same side for long periods every day. The ones we see most often in school-age children:
tur30-4: Always sitting at the desk leaning to the same side, against a wall or on one elbow
tur30-5: Sitting with the weight always on the same buttock, or always with one leg tucked underneath
tur30-6: Shifting the trunk to one side and dropping one shoulder while writing
tur30-7: Sitting in the same place in the classroom all year and always turning the same way to see the board
tur30-8: Always standing with the weight on the same leg
tur30-9: Always carrying a bag on one shoulder, or a heavy item or musical instrument on the same side
tur30-10: In a case-control study of 2,538 students (mean age 13) taking part in school screening in China, suspected scoliosis on screening was 31% less common in those who said they sat upright and 28% less common in those who regularly changed where they sat in class, while it was 40% more common in those whose school desk was too low for their height. No significant link was found with sitting leaning to the left or right. The habits were self-reported by the students, and scoliosis was not confirmed by X-ray.
tur30-11: In another study in China in which 90,635 students were screened, among the 1,458 students who had an X-ray, those with a habit of leaning or tilting to one side had about twice the likelihood of scoliosis, and those who sat slumped over the desk about 1.5 times; no link was found with the way the bag was carried. This is also a cross-sectional study: it is possible that a child with a curve already leans to one side.
tur30-12: In short: It has not been shown that one-sided habits on their own cause scoliosis; but some studies have found links with certain sitting habits, and these habits are also linked to back and low back pain.
tur30-13: In young people going through a growth spurt, one-sided habits such as always sitting at the desk leaning to the same side or against a wall, always putting the weight on the same buttock, or always carrying a bag on the same shoulder or a heavy item or musical instrument on the same side can make postural asymmetry more noticeable. When connective tissue flexibility is also present, as in benign joint hypermobility syndrome, we see that these asymmetries and back pain can be more marked. This does not mean that one-sided habits cause structural scoliosis; but it is a good reason to share the load between both sides during the growth years.
tur30-14: Try to sit at the desk with the weight evenly on both buttocks and the back supported; during long lessons and homework, get up and move around from time to time.
tur30-15: The desk and chair should suit the child's height: feet flat on the floor and elbows resting comfortably on the desk.
tur30-16: If possible, change where the child sits in class during the term, so they do not always turn the same way to see the board.
tur30-17: Do one-sided habits, heavy bags or poor posture cause scoliosis?
tur30-18: There is no strong evidence for this: the Scoliosis Research Society (SRS) states that heavy bags, poor posture and sport do not cause scoliosis or make a curve worse, and a study of 966 students in Portugal also found no link between bag weight or postural habits and scoliosis. However, some studies based on school screening in China found links between scoliosis and sitting leaning to one side or slumped over the desk, and desks unsuited to the child's height; these studies do not show cause and effect. A heavy bag can cause back pain, and poor sitting habits have also been linked to low back pain. In our clinical experience, we see that one-sided habits such as always sitting at the desk leaning to one side or always carrying a bag on the same shoulder can make postural asymmetry and pain more noticeable in young people going through a growth spurt and those with flexible connective tissue; so we recommend sharing the load between both sides.
